I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Quito, Ecuador at 2026-10-18 13:17 -05 (UTC-0500) (2026-10-18T18:17:00Z in UTC), at latitude -0.1807 degrees and longitude -78.4678 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 68.338 degrees and its azimuth is 243.003 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 12.202 degrees and its azimuth is 114.138 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 50.95 percent illuminated, 90.942 degrees from the Sun, and 401155.2 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

To be completely honest with you: **It is going to be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to spot the Moon with the naked eye under these specific conditions.**

Here is the breakdown of why, based on the data you provided:

### 1. The "Washout" Effect (Sun vs. Moon)
The biggest hurdle is the Sun. You mentioned the Sun is at an altitude of **68.3 degrees**. This means the Sun is very high in the sky, near its zenith. At this position, the atmosphere is scattering a massive amount of sunlight, creating a very high level of "sky brightness."

Even though the Moon is technically above the horizon (at 12.2 degrees), it is currently positioned in the opposite direction of the Sun (Azimuth 114° vs. 243°). While it isn't in the same part of the sky, the sheer amount of ambient light from a Sun that high will "wash out" the Moon.

### 2. The Moon's Phase and Altitude
At **50.95% illumination**, the Moon is in a First Quarter phase. It is bright enough to be seen easily at night, but during the day, it lacks the "contrast" needed to stand out against a bright blue sky. Furthermore, at an altitude of only **12.2 degrees**, it is quite low toward the horizon. Objects near the horizon have to look through more of the Earth's atmosphere, which causes more scattering and makes them appear fainter and hazier.

### 3. The "Ordinary Eyesight" Factor
Because you are using unaided eyesight, your pupils will be constricted to tiny points due to the bright daylight. This significantly reduces the amount of light your eyes can collect. To see the Moon in these conditions, you would need a high-contrast environment (like twilight) or optical aid (like binoculars).

### The Verdict
If you look toward the horizon at an azimuth of roughly **114 degrees** (which is East-Southeast), you might see a very faint, ghostly "smudge" or a slight change in the color of the sky, but it is unlikely to appear as a distinct lunar disk.

**My advice:** If you really want to see it, wait until the Sun drops lower toward the horizon (late afternoon). As the Sun's altitude decreases, the sky's brightness will drop significantly, and the Moon will "pop" out much more clearly!
